entries.note: [[see:Thomas Edison]] persuaded telephone companies to recommend opening calls with hello; people did not say hello before the telephone.
The phrase [[see:Thomas Edison]] encouraged people to end phone calls with, alongside starting them with [[see:hello]].
The telephone greeting [[see:Alexander Graham Bell]] wanted everyone to use instead of [[see:hello]].
Name for US telephone operators, because [[from:hello]] became so closely tied to telephone conversations.
Not an acronym for 'port out, starboard home', despite [[see:Chitty Chitty Bang Bang]]; no ticket bearing those words has ever been found.
Film blamed for spreading the false 'port out, starboard home' story behind [[see:posh]].
Not an acronym for 'ship high in transit'; it has Old and Middle English predecessors that meant exactly what it means today.
Another false acronym: it does not stand for 'to ensure promptness'.
A collective noun recorded in the old [[see:Book of St Albans]]; Jess has pet crows named Weatherwax, Hazel and Elphaba.
The collective noun for snails, according to the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Collective noun given to us by the [[see:Book of St Albans]].
Collective noun from the [[see:Book of St Albans]], one Jess especially loves.
A commonly confused word or phrase, an understandable mistake such as [[see:wreck havoc]], often involving fossil words; contrasted with [[see:malapropism]].
A more egregious word mix-up, named after [[from:Mrs. Malaprop]] of Sheridan's The Rivals; contrasted with an [[see:eggcorn]].
Mistake for 'wreak havoc', given as an example of an [[see:eggcorn]].
Character in Sheridan's The Rivals who makes outrageous mistakes such as [[see:pineapple]] for pinnacle; [[gave:malapropism]] is named after her.
Said by [[see:Mrs. Malaprop]] instead of pinnacle, an example of a [[see:malapropism]].
Words where English keeps the negative form but has lost the positive one, such as [[see:nonchalant]].
An English invention, not a French word, made by adding non- to a French-looking root meaning heat; nobody has ever been 'chalant'.
Based on Latin [[from:non plus]], 'no more': not knowing how to respond rather than simply confused.
Nautical: ships, especially pirates, approached under a friendly flag and revealed their real flag, or colours, at the last moment.
Literally 'star sailor', one of the words built on the nautical root.
Literally 'cosmos sailor', a counterpart of [[same-root:astronaut]].
Literally means seasickness, so feeling nauseated is feeling as if seasick.
Originally 'a numpire'; the N moved to the article, an example of [[see:rebracketing]].
Originally 'a napron', which lost its N to the article through [[see:rebracketing]].
Originally 'a nadder', which lost its N to the article through [[see:rebracketing]].
Originally 'an ewt'; it gained an N from the article, the reverse of [[see:umpire]].
When an N moves between the article and the noun, as in [[see:umpire]] and [[see:newt]].
Was never 'a norange' in English, though ancestors like [[from:naranja]] began with N; the colour is named after the fruit.
A blend like [[see:hangry]], coined in this sense by [[see:Lewis Carroll]], usually understood as a travel bag holding two words.
Hungry plus angry, given as an example of a [[see:portmanteau]].
[[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s blend of furious and fuming.
[[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s blend of slimy and lithe.
[[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s blend of chuckle and snort, now in common use.
[[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s blend of gallop and triumph, now in common use.
British name, from the same Latin [[from:coriandrum]] as American [[same-root:cilantro]]; one came through French, the other through Spanish.
American name for the leaves, the Spanish-derived form of [[from:coriandrum]]; a doublet of [[same-root:coriander]].
Means 'twice baked', almost identical to Italian [[same-root:biscotti]]; in America it is a kind of savoury scone.
The American word for what Brits call a [[see:biscuit]]; American cookies are usually softer.
Very hard, twice-baked Italian biscuits whose name is almost identical to [[same-root:biscuit]].
From a root meaning to sprout, shared with [[same-root:grass]], [[same-root:grow]] and [[same-root:graze]].
Shares its root with [[same-root:green]].
Shares its root with [[same-root:green]].
Shares its root with [[same-root:green]].
Old English name for the colour before [[see:orange]] stuck.
One of the earlier names for the colour now called [[see:orange]].
Another past name for the colour [[see:orange]].
From Greek [[from:galaxias kyklos]], 'milky circle', so 'the Milky Way galaxy' says the same thing twice.
Already the meaning of [[see:galaxy]], making 'Milky Way galaxy' a doubling up.
From Greek [[from:zodiakos kyklos]], 'circle of little animals', related to [[same-root:zoology]] and [[same-root:zoo]].
Related to [[same-root:zodiac]].
Related to [[same-root:zodiac]].
Old British word for a thousand million, lost when Britain adopted the American [[see:billion]] around the 1970s; Rob wants it back.
The American sense, one followed by nine zeros, which replaced British [[see:milliard]].
Modern word glossed by the lost words [[see:hubble-shubble]], [[see:bobbery]] and [[see:foofaraw]].
Modern word glossed by the lost words [[see:hubble-shubble]], [[see:bobbery]] and [[see:foofaraw]].
Modern word glossed by the lost words [[see:hubble-shubble]], [[see:bobbery]] and [[see:foofaraw]].
Antiquated word for a [[see:hullabaloo]] or [[see:kerfuffle]].
Antiquated word for a [[see:hullabaloo]] or [[see:brouhaha]].
Antiquated word for a fuss, which stuck in Jess's head in Rob's accent.
Words that survive only in a particular fixed phrase, such as [[see:shrift]] in [[see:short shrift]].
A fossil word surviving only in [[gave:short shrift]], originally meaning confession.
Originally giving a condemned criminal only a short time to confess before execution; it preserves [[from:shrift]].
Originally a Shakespearean phrase, literally blown up by your own [[from:petard]], so jokingly 'by your own fart bomb'.
A conical bomb used to breach fortifications, related to French [[from:pet]], fart.
Originally meant any food, hence [[see:green meat]], [[see:white meat]] and [[see:flesh meat]]; it also explains [[see:sweetmeats]].
Old term for vegetables, when [[see:meat]] meant any food.
Old term for dairy, when [[see:meat]] meant any food.
Old term for what we now call [[see:meat]].
Still in use, and explained by the old sense of [[see:meat]] as any food.
Literally someone you share bread with, related to [[same-root:panini]], [[same-root:empanada]] and [[same-root:pantry]].
A bready word related to [[same-root:companion]].
A bready word related to [[same-root:companion]].
Related to [[same-root:companion]]; pantries are bready too.
A word that is its own opposite.
Means the same thing as [[see:unraveled]], a fact left out of the contronyms episode.
Means the same as [[see:raveled]]; the word is on Rob's merch shirt.
Named after Civil War general [[from:Ambrose Burnside]]'s whiskers, then swapped round because people assumed it was a general term.
Civil War general with magnificent whiskers who gave his name to [[gave:sideburns]].
Named after [[from:Ceres]], the goddess of agriculture.
Named after the forest god [[from:Pan]], who supposedly drove people mad or was linked with the chaos of the wilds.
A word that reads the same in either direction, such as [[see:tattarrattat]].
The OED's longest palindrome at 12 letters, used by James Joyce in [[see:Ulysses]] for a knock at the door.
A word that spells another word backwards, like [[see:bonk]] and [[see:knob]]; also called an [[see:anadrome]].
Another name for a [[see:heteropalindrome]].
Spells [[see:knob]] backwards, an example of a [[see:heteropalindrome]].
Spells [[see:bonk]] backwards, an example of a [[see:heteropalindrome]].
Medieval insult for someone taking up too much space on the planet, an encumbrance on the world.
Jess's favourite ending, used to make insults and pejoratives, as in [[see:dullard]], [[see:braggart]] and [[see:bastard]].
Example of the insulting ending [[see:-ard]].
Example of the insulting ending [[see:-ard]].
Built with [[see:-ard]], it literally means a pack-saddle son, a child conceived while travelling.
The longest scientific name for an organism, found in a soil sample from the Welsh village of [[from:Llanfairpwllgwyngyll]].
Political term about disestablishing the Church of England, boosted when [[see:Gloria Lockerman]] spelled it on [[see:The $64,000 Question]].
Twelve-year-old who spelled [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]] correctly on a mid-20th-century game show.
Game show on which [[see:Gloria Lockerman]] spelled [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]].
Swedish village near Stockholm with more elements named after it than any other place: [[gave:yttrium]], [[gave:ytterbium]], [[gave:terbium]] and [[gave:erbium]].
Element named, not very creatively, after [[from:Ytterby]].
Element named after [[from:Ytterby]].
Element named after [[from:Ytterby]].
Element named after [[from:Ytterby]].

Element also found at [[see:Ytterby]].
Related to [[same-root:beryl]], the family of gemstones.
Gemstones including [[see:emerald]] and [[see:aquamarine]]; related to [[same-root:brilliant]] and [[same-root:beryllium]].
One of the [[see:beryl]] gemstones.
One of the [[see:beryl]] gemstones.
Listed among the [[see:beryl]] gemstones.
One of the [[see:beryl]] gemstones.
The element whose name connects [[see:beryl]] and [[see:brilliant]].
Has a silent H only by analogy with [[see:ghost]].
Has a silent H because Flemish printers who brought printing to England spelled it as in Flemish.
Formerly part of [[see:Tarrytown]]; renamed in 1996 after [[from:The Legend of Sleepy Hollow]] to attract spooky tourism, which worked.
Town where [[see:Washington Irving]] lived and of which [[see:Sleepy Hollow]] was formerly part.
Author of The Legend of Sleepy Hollow who lived in [[see:Tarrytown]]; also created [[see:Diedrich Knickerbocker]].
Originally meant satisfied, related to [[same-root:satisfied]] and sated; the current sense comes from having had enough.
Related to [[same-root:sad]], as are satiated and sated.
Often thought beautiful but literally 'black bile', one of the four humours of [[see:humorism]].
Theory of four humours governing health, behind [[see:melancholy]]; Rob calls it hilarious, as its name suggests.
Shares a root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:true]].
Shares a root meaning steadfast with [[same-root:tree]].
Originally called an [[see:urchin]].
Original name for the [[see:hedgehog]], which gave us [[gave:sea urchin]].
A 'sea hedgehog', named after the old sense of [[from:urchin]] because it looks like one.
German linguists concluded the British have 546 words for it, including [[see:cabbaged]], [[see:blottoed]] and [[see:flooded]].
One of the British words for [[see:drunk]].
One of the British words for [[see:drunk]]; Jess has used 'blotto'.
One of the British words for [[see:drunk]].
Rob's favourite of the expressions for being [[see:drunk]].
Means 'water of life', like [[equivalent:aquavit]] and [[equivalent:eau de vie]].
Spirit whose name means 'water of life', like [[equivalent:whiskey]].
Spirit whose name means 'water of life', like [[equivalent:whiskey]].
Means 'little water'.
Highest-scoring word in American-rules Scrabble, earning Michael Cresta 365 points in 2006; related to [[same-root:quixotic]].
Named after [[from:Don Quixote]].
Every sense, from a checkbox to a bank cheque, comes from chess, ultimately via [[from:checkmate]]; related to [[same-root:exchequer]].
Also from chess, like [[same-root:check]].
From Arabic and Persian [[from:shah mat]], 'the king dies' or 'the king cannot move'.
Originally meant the twittering of birds, understandable only to other birds, as jargon is only to insiders.
Much older than expected, a biblical term meaning working together, built like [[see:collaboration]] from Greek elements.
Identical in construction to [[see:synergy]], from Latin rather than Greek elements.
From Greek roots meaning to turn away; in possessives the missing letter is the E of Middle English -es; also a dramatic aside technique.
A hatmaker, originally a trader selling garments from [[from:Milan]], called Milaners.
Old English term for a carpenter, later replaced by a French word.
Old English term for a baker.
Old English term for a soldier.
Old English term for a builder.
Old English term for a mason, which Jess thinks still has legs.
Lost English word for a [[see:butcher]], replaced after the Norman Conquest.
Rob's favourite -wright word; likely a maker of sausages rather than trifle.
Used ironically by [[see:Ben Jonson]]; the -wright means someone who has wrought a play, not written one.
Most likely means fart, from Greek [[from:perdesthai]], to break wind, perhaps from the sound its wings make.
From French but ultimately from the same Germanic source as [[same-root:yule]].
Related to [[same-root:jolly]]; similar words still mean Christmas in the Scandinavian languages.
From 18th-century playwright [[see:John Dennis]], whose thunder sound effect was copied for another play after his own was cancelled.

entries.term: by the skin of your teeth
entries.note: From the Book of Job in the King James Bible, originally 'with the skin of my teeth'.
Originally hiding under someone's eaves to listen to conversations, which was a crime.
A variant of [[from:hoist]], to lift, with the same logic as [[see:lift]] meaning steal.
To lift into the air, the word [[gave:heist]] varies.
Used to mean steal, by the same logic as [[see:heist]].
Another robbery expression compared with [[see:heist]].
Means a 'swollen hundred'; its -sand is related to [[same-root:hundred]].
From old hund, a hundred, plus an ending originally meaning a count; related to [[same-root:thousand]].
From Arabic [[from:al-jabr]], a reunion of broken parts or restoration, originally used of setting bones.
Once called the hautboy in English; oboe is an Italian take on French [[from:hautbois]].
Named for its high register among woodwinds; it gave English hautboy and, via Italian, [[gave:oboe]].
In ancient Greek theatre the semicircular space where the chorus danced, literally 'the dancing place'; it also ends [[gave:karaoke]].
Means 'empty orchestra', its -oke a Japanese rendering of [[from:orchestra]].
From Old English for 'nose hole'; its ending is related to [[same-root:thrill]].
Originally meant to pierce or run someone through; related to the ending of [[same-root:nostril]].
Old English word for the head, a [[see:kenning]] like [[see:bone locker]].
Old English word for the body, a [[see:kenning]].
Combining two semi-unrelated words into a metaphorical image, as in [[see:brain locker]] and [[see:Beowulf]].
Means 'bee wolf', a [[see:kenning]] for a bear, perhaps because bears like honey.
Rhyme scheme [[see:Geoffrey Chaucer]] is credited with bringing into English; rhyme came from French, as Old English poetry used alliteration instead.
Itself an oxymoron, its Greek elements meaning sharp-dull or clever-stupid; related to [[same-root:moron]].
Calls someone dull or stupid, from Greek moros, the second element of [[same-root:oxymoron]].
Not really 'wise fool' but related to [[same-root:sophistry]]; sophomores at Oxford and Cambridge studied rhetoric.
From the sophists, philosophers known for rhetoric; related to [[same-root:sophomore]].
From Old English for 'day's eye', because it opens by day and closes at night.
From French [[from:dent de lion]], 'lion's tooth', for its jagged leaves; also called [[equivalent:milk witch]], [[equivalent:piss-a-bed]] and [[equivalent:canker wort]].
Another name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]].
Another name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]], matching French [[equivalent:pissenlit]].
Another name for the [[equivalent:dandelion]].
The French still call the [[equivalent:dandelion]] this.
Once known in English as the [[see:windfucker]], referring to its beating wings.
Old name for the [[see:kestrel]], from the rapid beating of its wings, since [[from:fuck]] meant to beat.
Once meant to beat something, explaining [[gave:windfucker]].
Meant donkey before backside, the donkey sense related to [[same-root:asinine]]; it merged with [[see:arse]], probably unrelated.
Coexisted in Old English with [[see:ass]] the donkey; the two have merged, though probably unrelated.
Literally 'like an ass', related to the donkey sense of [[same-root:ass]].
Short for [[from:logotype]], from Greek logos, word: originally a single piece of type for a whole word, so Apple's emblem isn't strictly one.
Printing term that [[gave:logo]] is shortened from.
From Japanese words for picture and character, [[unrelated:emotion]] and [[unrelated:emote]], though the resemblance likely helped it catch on.
Latin-derived word that [[see:emoji]] resembles but is unrelated to.
Latin-derived word that [[see:emoji]] resembles but is unrelated to.
Italian spelling with French pronunciation (French had an R), adopted when military historians became keen on Italian tactics.
Short for the woman's name [[from:Gunilda]], from Norse 'battle'; a 1330 Windsor Castle inventory names a large ballista Domina Gunilda.
A big cannon, also called Great Meg, another weapon given a woman's name like [[see:gun]].
Mag, a woman's name from Margaret, plus pie, an older word for the bird.
Shakespeare first used it for something other than coins in [[see:Hamlet]]: 'This is the very coinage of your brain.'
First appears in As You Like It, first describing weary eyes; one of Shakespeare's lack- compounds like [[see:lack-brain]].
One of Shakespeare's lack- compounds, like [[see:lackluster]].
One of Shakespeare's lack- compounds, like [[see:lackluster]].
A cutting Shakespearean lack- compound, like [[see:lackluster]].
In England the most expensive schools; in the US the cheapest.
Began as Cazeline after salesman John Cassell; counterfeiter John Boyd changed it to Gazeline, later reinterpreted as gas plus Latin oleum plus -ine.
British counterpart of American [[see:gasoline]].
American use for a liquid fuel, explained by [[from:gasoline]].
From hatmakers suffering mercury poisoning from the mercurous nitrate used to make felt hats.
From military planes' ball-shaped engine-control grips, pushed fully forward to speed up or dive; sometimes wrongly linked to [[see:balls out]].
From steam engine governors whose fly balls swing outward as the engine speeds up; same meaning as [[see:balls to the wall]].
The car company was SS Cars, for Swallow Sidecars, but renamed itself after the Second World War because of SS's Nazi associations.
Not inherently 'the end': first a ship's galley, then a train's galley or staff car, often but not always at the back.
Named after the French city of [[from:Nîmes]], 'de Nîmes'.
Named after the Italian city of [[from:Genoa]], from an old English spelling of it.
From [[from:knickerbockers]]; became a nickname for [[see:bloomers]], then crossed to Britain as women's underwear.
Named after [[from:Diedrich Knickerbocker]], shown wearing Dutch-style trousers billowing around the knee; [[gave:knickers]] comes from it.
[[see:Washington Irving]]'s New York Dutch caricature, illustrated in knee-billowing trousers, who gave [[gave:knickerbockers]].
Named not for their shape but after [[from:Amelia Bloomer]], who advocated the garment.
Suffragist and women's rights activist ridiculed in the media for promoting [[gave:bloomers]].

entries.term: the writing is on the wall
entries.note: From the Bible: disembodied handwriting on [[see:Belshazzar]]'s wall predicted his death that night, and he died.
Biblical king whose death was foretold by [[see:the writing is on the wall]].
Coined in John Milton's [[see:Paradise Lost]] as Satan's palace in Hell; literally 'all demons', hence chaos today.
Originally an evil spirit that stole and ate children from their beds; also a word for a scarecrow.
Not a nocturnal horse but a demon that sits on sleepers, like an incubus; compared with [[see:bugbear]].
Not a spoonerism of [[unrelated:flutterby]]; from myths that butterflies eat butter, or their yellow colour; compare Dutch [[see:boterschijte]].
Popularly but wrongly thought to be the source of [[see:butterfly]].
Old Dutch name for the [[see:butterfly]], referring to its yellow poo.
Originally a WWII bomb thought able to destroy a whole block; the first film called one was [[see:Bombardier]].
First film to be described as a [[see:blockbuster]].
Coined by [[see:The Simpsons]], a mostly nonsensical word that in context means satisfactory.
Coined by [[see:The Simpsons]] alongside [[see:cromulent]].
Show that coined [[see:embiggen]] and [[see:cromulent]].
A unit in a medieval system dividing the hour into pricks, [[see:moment]]s, [[see:ounce]]s and [[see:atom]]s.
A unit in the medieval division of the hour alongside [[see:prick]], [[see:ounce]] and [[see:atom]].
A unit in the medieval division of the hour alongside [[see:prick]], [[see:moment]] and [[see:atom]].
Means 'unsplittable'; there were 22,560 atoms in a medieval hour.
Related to [[same-root:moon]] and to measurement words like [[same-root:meter]], [[same-root:dimension]], [[same-root:menstrual]] and [[same-root:semester]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
A measurement word related to [[same-root:month]].
A measurement word related to [[same-root:month]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
Sounds as if it means half but means six months; related to [[same-root:month]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
Came in after the Norman Conquest, replacing [[see:flesh monger]]; named for dealing in goat meat, its butch- related to [[same-root:buck]].
Related to [[same-root:butcher]]; not a goat in English today, but compare Afrikaans [[same-root:bok]].
Afrikaans for a goat-like animal, cognate with [[same-root:buck]], as in [[see:springbok]].
A little jumping goat-like animal, containing [[see:bok]].
From French [[from:bouder]], to pout or sulk: a room where a woman withdraws to be alone, literally a grumpy room.
Called [[see:boudoir]] in French, supposedly because one might enjoy such a light dessert in one's boudoir.
Originally a physical ticket for another baseball game when yours was rained off.
From Greek [[from:meteoron]], a thing high in the air: the study of all atmospheric phenomena, not of [[see:meteor]]s.
Originally anything visible high in the sky, such as storms, rainbows, auroras or shooting stars.
Named after a Czech valley: from [[from:Joachimsthaler]], coins of silver mined at Joachimsthal, now [[see:Jáchymov]].
Town in Bohemia formerly called Joachimsthal, whose silver coins gave [[gave:Joachimsthaler]] and so [[gave:dollar]].
Coins of silver mined at Joachimsthal ([[from:Jáchymov]]), the source of [[gave:dollar]].
From [[from:Moneta]], epithet of [[see:Juno]], whose Roman temple stood near where money was minted; related to [[same-root:mint]].
Like [[same-root:money]], from [[from:Moneta]], Juno's epithet, from her temple near Rome's mint.
Epithet of [[see:Juno]], whose temple stood near Rome's mint; it gave [[gave:money]] and [[gave:mint]].
